extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, marketers, business owners and communicators seeking media coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and shaping announcements, press releases, and pitches so journalists deem them newsworthy and more likely to place coverage. Emphasizes traditional news values plus digital-era factors (algorithms, visuals, data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (The Power of “Now”)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness is perhaps the most fundamental element of newsworthiness: news, by definition, is new information. When something happens recently or is happening now, it creates urgency and relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to leverage timeliness: Connect your story to recent events or trending topics; release information promptly—delays can kill newsworthiness; frame ongoing situations with fresh angles or developments; time announcements strategically to align with relevant dates. Example: Rapidly positioning a CEO as an expert after a major data breach produced coverage within 24 hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact (Scope and Significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact measures how many people are affected by a story and how significantly they’re affected. Stories with broader reach and deeper consequences attract more attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to demonstrate impact: Quantify number of people affected (use specific numbers when possible); illustrate depth of effect on individuals or groups; show broader implications beyond the immediate situation; connect micro trends to macro consequences. Example: Focusing on a healthcare platform's potential to reduce errors affecting 400,000 patients annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity (The Local Connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proximity refers to how close a story is to the audience—geographically and psychologically. People care more about events happening in their community or that affect groups they identify with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to utilize proximity: Localize broader stories for specific markets; highlight regional implications of national trends; create market-specific data/examples when pitching local media; demonstrate psychological proximity through relatable circumstances. Example: Customized press releases emphasizing local job creation for each new retail location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence (The Power of Notable Names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving well-known individuals, brands, or institutions inherently generate more interest because they come with built-in audience attention and perceived importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to incorporate prominence: Highlight connections to recognized brands/people/institutions; feature quotes or endorsements from industry leaders; mention partnerships with prominent organizations; reference previous prestigious coverage. Example: Announcing advisory board members from JPMorgan/Goldman to elevate a startup announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (The Allure of the Unusual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual, unexpected, or novel events capture attention; true novelty must be genuine and substantive rather than marketing hyperbole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to emphasize novelty: Identify truly unique aspects (first, only, largest, etc.); challenge conventional wisdom with surprising data; highlight unexpected approaches or outcomes; present familiar issues from genuinely new perspectives. Example: Focusing on biodegradable packaging made from agricultural waste as a surprising angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict (Tension and Resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving conflict, controversy, or tension draw interest by introducing stakes, competing perspectives, or struggles that engage audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to present conflict: Frame challenges and solutions as narratives; present different perspectives on controversial issues; highlight competitive dynamics or market disruptions; document struggles and eventual triumphs. Example: Framing rising medication costs vs. patient access to humanize policy issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Interest (Emotional Connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that evoke emotion, illustrate universal experiences, or showcase remarkable human achievements create deeper audience engagement and make abstract issues relatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to cultivate human interest: Include personal stories and testimonials; highlight individual experiences within broader trends; showcase compelling visuals of people behind statistics; connect technical innovations to human impact. Example: Focusing on customer service reps enabled to do more meaningful work by automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic Amplification (Digital-era News Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social platforms' algorithms can influence what becomes news by amplifying stories based on engagement metrics; understanding algorithmic incentives helps predict traction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AI/data tools to analyze engagement patterns and craft stories optimized for algorithmic amplification while maintaining journalistic integrity. Consider formats and hooks likely to trigger shares, comments, and other engagement signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Participation (Interactive Newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern news often involves audience interaction—comments, shares, polls, and user-generated content—which can extend visibility and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stories to encourage participation (questions, polls, submissions). Stories that invite audience interaction often receive greater visibility and longer coverage cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Storytelling Imperative
rubrics_metrics.description: In a visual-first media environment, compelling imagery or video dramatically increases a story’s chance of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include high-quality visual assets with pitches; 65% higher placement likelihood for pitches including visuals (per internal data). Develop photos, video, charts, or other media tailored to publication needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-Driven Narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists increasingly value stories backed by original data or research, which provide credibility and exclusive content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct newsworthy surveys or analyze internal data to generate unique insights. Use original data as the foundation for stories and thought leadership; present surprising findings and methodology transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Newsworthy Score Matrix (Scoring Guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proprietary scoring system: rate the story 1–5 on each key factor (Timeliness, Impact, Proximity, Prominence, Novelty, Conflict, Human Interest) to assess coverage potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring thresholds: Stories scoring 25+ (out of 35) typically have strong potential for broad coverage; 18–24 may secure targeted placements; below 18 likely need strengthening or belong on owned channels. Use scores to prioritize which elements to strengthen before pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist Perspective Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Put yourself in a journalist’s position by asking critical questions journalists use to evaluate pitches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key questions: Why would their audience care about this story right now? What unique information or angle does this provide? How easy have you made it for them to cover this story? What supporting elements (data, visuals, interviews) are available? How does this fit with their publication’s typical content? Use answers to identify and fix gaps before pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing Importance with Newsworthiness (Common Mistake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating something important internally as automatically newsworthy externally is a frequent error—journalists care about audience relevance, not internal significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming internal milestones are newsworthy; add elements (impact, novelty, prominence, localization) that demonstrate external relevance. Example: A new office is not newsworthy unless tied to significant job creation or unique design features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burying the Lead (Common Mistake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hiding the most newsworthy element within less compelling details reduces the chance of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and lead with the strongest news angle. Restructure announcements to highlight the most compelling element up front; remove or de-emphasize minor details that distract from the main news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing Timely Connections (Common Mistake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to connect a story to current events, trends, or conversations can undermine its appeal even if other elements are strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor the news cycle and time pitches to contextual relevance; look for angles tying your story to breaking news or ongoing trends to increase receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglecting the “So What?” Factor (Common Mistake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every successful news story answers why the information matters—without that clear significance, pitches fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorously test the 'So what?' for each pitch; explicitly state implications and relevance for the target audience in the lead and pitch materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming Ordinary Updates: Data Transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting internal metrics into newsworthy insights by analyzing trends, making comparisons, or identifying surprising patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn routine metrics into reports or studies (e.g., quarterly industry trends) that generate repeat coverage and position the organization as a thought leader. Example: Anonymized user data analysis produced a quarterly report that gained trade press coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming Ordinary Updates: Localization Strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating market-specific angles from broader trends so regional media find stories relevant to their audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize nationwide promotions or trends by emphasizing regional preferences, local impacts, or tailored data to secure coverage across multiple local outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming Ordinary Updates: Human Impact Focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting from technical or business details to personal stories that illustrate broader points, thereby increasing emotional resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange interviews with affected individuals, use testimonials, and foreground human consequences to turn technical announcements into features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming Ordinary Updates: Expert Commentary Positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing organizational leaders as expert sources who can provide valuable perspective on breaking news and trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop thought leadership and media training; proactively offer experts for commentary on relevant stories to become a regular source for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building Relationships with Journalists (Practices for Better Coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term media relationships increase the ability to secure coverage; relationship-building practices are a core component of newsworthiness strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key practices: Personalized research on reporters' beats and recent articles; value-first engagement (provide helpful info/connections without immediate asks); request and integrate feedback after rejections; consistent reliability—deliver accurate information and timely access to sources. Maintain detailed journalist profiles and match stories carefully rather than mass-distributing pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic Approach to Crafting Newsworthy Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeatable process combining research, amplification, contextual mapping, format variation, and targeted distribution to develop newsworthy angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: Scientific media analysis (identify recent coverage patterns); news value amplification (combine multiple factors rather than relying on one); contextual relevance mapping (monitor trends to time pitches); multi-format content development (press releases, concise pitches, visual assets); targeted distribution strategy (match stories to journalists based on beats). Use this system to increase placement success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring Newsworthiness and Coverage Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate success beyond placements by assessing coverage prominence, message inclusion, reach, engagement, and business outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics to track: placement count and prominence (feature vs. mention), inclusion of key messages, reach to target audiences, engagement metrics (shares, comments), use of visual assets, journalist feedback, resulting website traffic or lead generation. Combine these to assess whether a story was truly newsworthy.
